Apprenticeship works because the work is visible. Methodological judgment is not.
Most of what makes a good analytic decision — why this coding scheme, why this
window, why this model and not that one — happens where students cannot see it,
and so my teaching is largely about externalising it: working through real
decisions in front of students, on real data, including the ones I get wrong.

The same principle generates how I assess. You cannot coach reasoning you cannot
observe. So rather than asking only for the product, I ask for the evidence that
teaching needed anyway — the process that produced it.

## Teaching with and about AI

In my honours research-methods unit, students meet the AI tools that now mediate
the research process early — ChatGPT, Claude, Scopus AI, NotebookLM, Perplexity.
We model appropriate use in class and then analyse the tools critically, as
instruments with particular affordances and constraints.

Students may use GenAI on assignments provided they **declare, describe and
reflect** on that use, and assessed products are supplemented with in-class
demonstrations of ownership — pitches, discussions, presentations. Student
frustration at documenting their AI use, and my own frustration reading loosely
structured records of it, was part of what prompted the *Trace* browser
extension.

::: {.panel}
Monash doctoral candidates are research-only, with no required coursework, and
are supervised by a committee of a **main supervisor**, who directs the project —
the equivalent of a US advisor — and associate supervisors.
:::

How that works in practice is deliberately layered: weekly one-on-one meetings
with main supervisees, weekly project-team meetings, and monthly lab meetings
that mix new and foundational topics, works in progress, and time that is simply
social. Students own their projects and mentor more junior students — which is
how the practice gets passed on rather than merely described.

## Methods workshops

For the last seven years I have run methods workshops for doctoral and
early-career researchers, most regularly **Advanced ENA and rENA** at the
International Conference on Quantitative Ethnography, every year from ICQE19
through ICQE26. Others include:

- *A workshop on writing in quantitative ethnography* — ICQE26, Hiroshima (with
  D. W. Shaffer and A. R. Ruis)
- *Integrating Quantitative Ethnography Methods to Support Learning Analytics in
  the Age of Artificial Intelligence* — LAK24, Kyoto
- *Techniques for Investigating Collaboration with Multimodal Approaches* — ISLS
  Annual Meeting 2023, Montreal
- *Creating, refining, and validating automated discourse codes: An introduction
  to nCoder and rho* — CSCL 2019, Lyon; earlier versions at LSGS and ICLS

I have also taught a **Quantitative Ethnography Masterclass Series** — six
invited lectures across National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University and National
Central University (Taiwan), Seoul National University (South Korea), and Osaka
and Senshu Universities (Japan).
